n: Be careful not to do your good deeds just to be seen by others; then there’s no reward from God. Jesus now addresses motives in three acts of devotion: giving, praying, and fasting.

f.g: Gifts to the poor; also good deeds generally (some manuscripts say “righteousness”).

n: When you give, don’t trumpet it like the hypocrites in synagogues and streets who want praise. They already have their reward — people’s applause, nothing more.

f.g: Greek hypokritēs — a stage actor wearing a mask.
Paid in full — the attention they wanted is all they get.

n: When you give, don’t let your left hand know what your right is doing — keep it quiet, even from yourself, avoiding self-congratulation.

f.w: let not thy left hand know
f.g: A picture of giving so naturally that you don’t keep score.

n: Give in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you.

f.w: thy Father which seeth in secret

n: When you pray, don’t be like hypocrites who love to pray on street corners to be seen.

f.g: Standing was a normal posture for prayer.

f.w: that they may be seen of men

n: Instead, go into your private room, shut the door, and pray to your Father in secret. He will reward you. Private prayer builds a real relationship with God.

f.g: An inner room or storeroom — a private space.

n: Don’t babble on with empty, repeated phrases like the pagans, who think they’ll be heard for using many words.

f.g: Meaningless babbling; mechanical, thoughtless words.

n: Your Father already knows what you need before you ask. Prayer isn’t informing God; it aligns our will with His.

f.w: your Father knoweth what things ye have need of

n: Jesus gives a pattern for prayer, not a script to repeat mechanically. It begins by addressing God as our Father in heaven and honoring His name as holy.

f.g: In this way — a model, not a formula.
Treated as holy, honored.

f.w: Our Father which art in heaven

n: Pray for God’s kingdom to come and His will to be done on earth as in heaven. Our wishes yield to His. (The Nephite version of the prayer omits “Thy kingdom come.”)
Ask for what we need today — one day at a time — trusting God as Israel trusted for manna.

f.g: The Greek word may mean “bread for today” or “for tomorrow.” This line is omitted in 3 Nephi 13.

n: Ask forgiveness for our debts (sins) as we forgive those who owe us. Sin is pictured as a debt we can’t pay.

f.g: Sins, moral debts; Luke 11:4 uses “sins.”

n: Ask God to keep us from temptation and rescue us from evil. The closing praise of His kingdom, power, and glory forever is absent in some early manuscripts but appears in 3 Nephi 13:13.

f.g: JST: “And suffer us not to be led into temptation.”

n: Jesus explains one line: if you forgive others, your Father will forgive you.

f.g: Wrongs, offenses.

f.w: if ye forgive men their trespasses

n: But if you refuse to forgive, God won’t forgive you. Forgiving others opens our own hearts to receive forgiveness.

f.w: if ye forgive not men their trespasses

n: When you fast, don’t look gloomy like the hypocrites, who make their faces miserable so others notice. That’s all the reward they get.

f.g: Leave faces unwashed, put on ashes — making a show of fasting.

n: When you fast, groom yourself normally — oil your hair and wash your face.

f.g: Put oil on your hair — normal daily grooming, a sign of gladness.

n: Then no one but your Father will know you’re fasting, and He will reward you. Fasting is between us and God.

f.w: thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly

n: Don’t store up treasures on earth, where moths eat clothes, rust (or decay) destroys, and thieves break in. Earthly wealth is fragile.

f.g: Corrosion or decay of any kind.
Literally “dig through” — mud-brick walls.

n: Store up treasures in heaven instead, where nothing can destroy or steal them.
Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. What we value most directs our affections.
The eye is the body’s lamp. If your eye is “single” — focused, generous, clear — your whole life is full of light.

f.g: Healthy, undivided, sincere; also suggests generosity.

f.w: if therefore thine eye be single

n: But if your eye is “evil” — greedy, envious — your whole life is dark. And if your inner light has become darkness, how deep that darkness is!

f.g: Diseased; in Jewish idiom, an “evil eye” meant greed or stinginess.

n: No one can serve two masters. You can’t serve both God and money. Ultimately we choose who rules us.

f.g: Aramaic for wealth or possessions, here personified as a rival god.

f.w: No man can serve two masters

n: So don’t be anxious about food, drink, or clothing. Isn’t life more than food, and the body more than clothes? In 3 Nephi, Jesus directed this especially to the Twelve He called to full-time ministry.

f.g: Don’t be anxious or worry (old English “thought” meant anxiety).

f.w: Take no thought for your life

n: Look at the birds: they don’t plant, harvest, or store, yet your Father feeds them. You are worth far more.

f.g: Birds.

n: Can worrying add a single hour to your life? Worry accomplishes nothing.

f.w: add one cubit unto his stature
f.g: A cubit is about 18 inches; the phrase may mean adding height or a little time to one’s life.

n: Why worry about clothes? Look how wildflowers grow — they don’t work or spin thread.

f.g: Wildflowers, perhaps anemones or poppies that carpet Galilee in spring.
Make thread for weaving cloth.

n: Yet not even King Solomon in all his splendor was dressed as beautifully as one of them.
If God dresses short-lived wild grass so beautifully, won’t He much more care for you, you of little faith?

f.g: Dried grass was used as fuel.

n: So don’t worry, saying, “What will we eat, drink, or wear?”

f.g: With what.

n: Those without faith chase after all these things, but your Father knows you need them.

f.g: Here, those who don’t know God.

n: Seek first God’s kingdom and His righteousness, and everything else will be provided. The JST reads “seek ye first to build up the kingdom of God.” Priorities matter.

f.w: seek ye first the kingdom of God

n: Don’t worry about tomorrow; it will bring its own concerns. Each day has enough trouble of its own. Live faithfully one day at a time.

f.w: Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof
f.g: Each day has enough trouble; don’t borrow tomorrow’s.
